guidance_items.text: German capitalizes ALL nouns, so capitalization alone is never evidence of a person name. Every rule must use at least one extra signal: (a) an academic or professional title (Dr., Mag., DI, Dipl.-Ing., Ing., Prof., MMag., Dkfm., MBA, BSc, MSc, LL.M.), (b) a salutation (Herr, Frau), (c) a role or context anchor (Richter/in, Vorsitzende/r, Beisitzer/in, Schriftführer/in, Rechtsanwalt, Steuerberater/in, Beschwerdeführer/in, Geschäftsführer/in, 'vertreten durch', 'z.H.', 'geb.'), or (d) a very specific name structure (e.g. an initial followed by a surname, 'A. Huber').

Do NOT write generic patterns like two consecutive capitalized words, or a single capitalized word on its own. These match ordinary German nouns, legal terms, authorities and place names, and they destroy precision.

Never label as PERSON: authorities and courts (Finanzamt, Bundesfinanzgericht, Verwaltungsgerichtshof, Senat, Magistrat), organisations (anything ending in GmbH, AG, KG, OG, e.U., Verein, Stiftung, or 'Firma ...'), places and street names, months, weekdays, legal terms (Bescheid, Beschwerde, Erkenntnis, Abgabe, Einkommensteuer), or role nouns that appear without a name ('der Beschwerdeführer' alone is not a person name).

Name components must allow German characters: use [A-ZÄÖÜ][a-zäöüß]+ instead of [A-Z][a-z]+. Support hyphenated names (Müller-Lüdenscheidt), multi-part surnames with lowercase particles (von, van, de, zu), and both orders 'Vorname Nachname' and 'Nachname Vorname'.

Prefer several narrow, high-precision rules (one per anchor type) over one broad rule. A rule that fires on fewer cases but is almost always right is better than one with high recall and many false positives.
